narrative:
The model estimated a 68.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, the assessment found failure more likely than success, and that estimate is why your application was denied.

The strongest factor was your Year 3 class-rank position: you were in the 2nd decile, while accepted students averaged around the 5.79 decile. Because this was the most influential item and it pointed toward bar-exam failure, it weighed heavily against admission. The second most important factor was your LSAT score. Your score of 37 was essentially at the accepted-student average of 37.18, and it actually pushed the prediction slightly toward passing rather than failing. The third factor was your Year 1 class-rank position: you were in the 3rd decile versus an accepted average near the 6th decile, and this also pushed toward failure.

Your gender and race were not used in the prediction. To improve a future application, focus on the areas the assessment treated as risks: raise your academic standing, especially later-year class rank, and seek advising on bar-exam preparation. You could also retake the LSAT if you believe you can improve, gather evidence of academic improvement, and reapply after strengthening your record.
